say.text: A 58-year-old man has a tense, tender groin lump that will not go back. He is vomiting and his pulse is fast.
What is your first step?

choices.label: Resuscitate, then take him to emergency surgery
Attempt gentle, then firm, manual reduction first
Order a groin ultrasound before deciding on surgery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a tense, tender, irreducible swelling with vomiting means for the bowel inside it, not for the lump.
Reducing it feels like the reflex, since most groin lumps do go back.
Tense, tender, irreducible with vomiting means strangulation. Forceful taxis can push gangrenous bowel back, or reduce the sac and contents en masse.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the signs again: they mean the bowel is at risk before any reduction.

say.text: Imaging feels thorough, and ultrasound is the test people reach for in any groin problem.
A clinically evident hernia is a clinical diagnosis, and here the bowel's viability comes first. What would a scan change in the next ten minutes?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the cases: imaging answers an uncertain lump, not a strangulated one.

say.text: Resuscitate, then emergency surgery. Strangulation means the bowel may be non-viable and need resection.
The bowel decides the next step, so reduction waits.
Same patient, now the mechanism.
Why is forceful reduction avoided when strangulation is suspected?

choices.label: Pain relief cannot show whether the bowel is still alive
It can push dead bowel back or cause reduction en masse
It turns a reducible hernia into an irreducible one
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what could be inside the sac, and what happens to it if it is pushed back into the abdomen.
Analgesia feels like the sensible step before any manipulation, so it seems to make taxis acceptable.
Pain relief does not show whether the bowel is alive, so the risk of pushing dead bowel back stays.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the danger is the bowel, not the pain.

say.text: Taxis is meant to make the hernia go back, so the risk seems to be getting stuck afterwards.
The danger is the bowel. Forceful reduction can push gangrenous bowel back, or reduce sac and contents together with the constriction still there.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what happens to dead bowel that goes back inside.

say.text: Forceful taxis can push gangrenous bowel back, or reduce sac and contents en masse with the constriction still present.
Strangulation is treated by emergency surgery with resection of non-viable bowel.
A 6-month-old boy has a reducible right groin swelling that appears on crying.
His surgeon plans the operation. Which plan is right?

choices.label: Excise the sac, then darn the posterior wall with sutures
Excise the sac alone by high ligation, no wall repair
Excise the sac, then reinforce the posterior wall with mesh
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the defect, not the operation: what is a child's sac, and how strong is his posterior wall?
Tempting: a repair that closes the back wall as well looks more thorough, as it does in adults.
A child's posterior wall is normal, so the extra suture line fixes nothing. The problem is the open sac, which herniotomy closes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but a child is not a small adult with a weak wall. The operation follows the defect.

say.text: Tempting: mesh feels like the safe reinforcement whatever the age.
The wall is not the weak point in a child, so mesh has nothing to reinforce. Herniotomy alone is the repair.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age qualifier: mesh answers an adult's weak wall.

say.text: In a child the defect is a patent processus vaginalis over a normal posterior wall, so removing the sac cures it.
Herniotomy alone, with no posterior wall repair, is the operation of choice.
A 35-year-old man has a primary, reducible right inguinal hernia. His surgeon has no laparoscopic training.
Which repair do you choose?

choices.label: Open Bassini repair, the classic tissue repair
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Match the operation to the surgeon's training and to the qualifiers: primary, unilateral, reducible.
Laparoscopic repair feels like the modern default, so newer seems better for any hernia.
Its place depends on the qualifiers. It suits bilateral or recurrent hernias, and primary unilateral ones in experienced hands. Which detail here is about the surgeon?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember laparoscopy is not the default; the qualifiers decide.

say.text: Bassini is the name you remember for classic open repair, and older PYQs expected it.
Current practice is Lichtenstein mesh repair for an adult. Bassini sutures the conjoint tendon under tension. Does this stem ask for the older key or for current practice?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair the old key with the new: Bassini was expected, Lichtenstein is the standard.

say.text: Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair is the standard open repair for an adult.
A surgeon without laparoscopic training points to the open route.
A peer plans the repair of a 50-year-old man's primary, reducible, unilateral hernia. His surgeon is trained in open repair. One step is wrong.
1. Examine: clinically evident. 2. Bassini repair as the standard open repair. 3. Warn of ilioinguinal nerve injury. 4. Discharge next day.
Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 1: no imaging for a clinically evident hernia
Step 2: Bassini as the standard open repair
Step 3: warn of ilioinguinal nerve injury
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which open repair current practice uses for a primary adult hernia, and what the older key expected.
Tempting: a groin you cannot see into makes a scan feel careful.
A clinically evident hernia is a clinical diagnosis, so step 1 is right and imaging would not change the plan.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember imaging is for an occult or uncertain lump.

say.text: Tempting: thigh numbness after groin surgery makes the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve feel like the risk.
In open repair the ilioinguinal nerve is the one at risk; the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is the laparoscopic risk. Step 3 is right.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie the nerve to the approach: the field of dissection decides.

say.text: Step 2 is the error. Bassini is the older key; current practice is Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair.
Steps 1 and 3 are right: a visible hernia needs no imaging, and open repair puts the ilioinguinal nerve at risk.
Which patient most clearly favours a laparoscopic repair?

choices.label: A fit adult with bilateral inguinal hernias
A primary unilateral hernia, surgeon untrained in laparoscopy
A 70-year-old man unfit for a general anaesthetic
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Laparoscopy is chosen for particular qualifiers, not for the hernia alone. Which option holds one?
Laparoscopy feels like the modern choice, so a surgeon may reach for it for any hernia.
A primary unilateral hernia does not favour it, and without training the open Lichtenstein repair is the standard.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember laparoscopy is not the default; the qualifiers decide.

say.text: Laparoscopy looks gentler, so an elderly patient may seem a good candidate.
Laparoscopic repair needs general anaesthesia, so an unfit patient is the wrong candidate.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember a general anaesthetic is a cost of laparoscopy, not a reason for it.

say.text: Bilateral hernias favour laparoscopic repair, and so does recurrence after an open repair.
It needs general anaesthesia and a learning curve, so it is chosen for these qualifiers, not for every hernia.
You counsel a patient about the nerve most at risk in open repair and in laparoscopic repair.
Which pairing is correct?

choices.label: Open: ilioinguinal; laparoscopic: lateral femoral cutaneous
Open: lateral femoral cutaneous; laparoscopic: ilioinguinal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where each approach dissects: through the groin from the front, or from inside the abdomen. Which nerve sits there?
The ilioinguinal nerve is the famous groin nerve, so it feels like the answer for every repair.
It is the nerve most injured in open repair, but laparoscopy puts the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve at risk. Does the approach change where the dissection runs?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember one nerve for every repair is the trap: the approach decides.

say.text: Both nerves lie in the groin, so a swap looks like a simple slip of memory.
Ilioinguinal is the open-repair nerve and lateral femoral cutaneous is the laparoscopic one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which approach works from the front of the groin.

say.text: Open repair most often injures the ilioinguinal nerve, with numbness over the root of the penis, anterior scrotum and upper medial thigh.
Laparoscopic repair most often injures the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, causing meralgia paraesthetica.
Three weeks after a TEP repair, a man has burning pain and tingling over the front and side of his thigh, with no weakness.
Which nerve is injured?

choices.label: Femoral nerve, the main nerve of the thigh
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The loss is skin sensation over the thigh, with no weakness. Which nerve supplies that skin and sits in the laparoscopic field?
Ilioinguinal is the nerve you associate with groin repairs, so it feels like the nerve for any repair.
Its injury causes numbness at the root of the penis, the scrotum and the upper medial thigh, not burning over the lateral thigh. This repair was laparoscopic.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match the setting: open repair, ilioinguinal; laparoscopic, lateral femoral cutaneous.

say.text: The femoral nerve is the big thigh nerve, so it seems the nerve of a thigh complaint.
A femoral nerve injury would weaken the thigh; this loss is sensory over the skin. The nerve most at risk in laparoscopic repair is the lateral femoral cutaneous.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask whether the problem is weakness or burning skin, and which approach was used.

say.text: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury causes burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral thigh, called meralgia paraesthetica.
It is the nerve most at risk in laparoscopic repair.
After a TAPP repair, a man has chronic groin pain and thigh numbness. A tack was placed lateral to the gonadal vessels, below the iliopubic tract.
Which triangle did the tack enter?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether this tack would catch vessels or nerves, and which triangle holds which.
Tempting: both triangles are no-tack zones, so doom feels like the right one.
The doom triangle holds the external iliac vessels. This tack sat lateral to the gonadal vessels, on the nerve side, in the triangle of pain.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so split the pair: vessels belong to doom, nerves to pain.

say.text: The triangle of pain lies lateral to the gonadal vessels and below the iliopubic tract, and holds nerves including the lateral femoral cutaneous.
The triangle of doom holds the external iliac vessels: vessels to doom, nerves to pain.
A 30-year-old athlete has chronic groin pain but no visible lump. An occult hernia is suspected.
Which test do you order first?

choices.label: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test is first for an uncertain groin swelling, and which follows only if it is inconclusive.
CT is the most advanced test on the list, so it looks like the thorough choice.
CT is for complicated or obscure presentations, such as suspected obstruction or strangulation in an obese patient. This is not one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the order: ultrasound first, MRI if inconclusive.

say.text: Herniography sounds purpose-built for a hidden hernia.
It is a historical investigation, largely replaced by cross-sectional imaging.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the exam answer: ultrasonography, with MRI if inconclusive.

say.text: Ultrasonography is the first test for an occult hernia or an uncertain groin swelling.
MRI is more sensitive if ultrasound is inconclusive.
Which pairing of term and meaning is correct?

choices.label: Herniorrhaphy is sac excision plus a mesh repair
Hernioplasty is sac excision plus own-tissue repair
Herniotomy is sac excision; hernioplasty adds mesh
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Order the terms by what is added to the sac excision: nothing, the patient's own tissue, or a mesh.
Tempting: herniorrhaphy sounds like the full modern repair, so it feels like the mesh one.
Herniorrhaphy uses the patient's own tissue. Mesh makes it hernioplasty.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so sort by what is added: tissue or mesh.

say.text: Tempting: hernioplasty sounds like the general word for any repair of the wall.
Hernioplasty means reinforcement with a prosthetic mesh. Own-tissue repair is herniorrhaphy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so sort by what is added: tissue or mesh.

say.text: Herniotomy is sac excision. Herniorrhaphy adds repair of the posterior wall with the patient's own tissue.
Hernioplasty reinforces the posterior wall with a prosthetic mesh.
A surgeon excises the sac and places polypropylene mesh over the posterior wall.
Which statement is correct?

choices.label: It is a herniotomy, because the sac was excised
It is a herniorrhaphy, because the wall was repaired
It is a hernioplasty, because mesh reinforces the wall
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the wall was reinforced with, and which term names that material.
Tempting: the sac is excised in every repair, so herniotomy seems to name the operation.
Herniotomy is sac excision alone, without wall reinforcement. A mesh over the wall makes it hernioplasty.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so sort by what is added: nothing, tissue or mesh.

say.text: Tempting: herniorrhaphy is the classic word for a wall repair, so it feels right for any wall repair.
Herniorrhaphy uses the patient's own tissue. Reinforcement with a prosthetic mesh is hernioplasty.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the wall was repaired with.

say.text: Hernioplasty is reinforcement of the posterior wall with a prosthetic mesh, most often polypropylene.
Herniorrhaphy adds the patient's own tissue, and herniotomy is the sac alone.

cards.q: First step in a tense, tender, irreducible groin lump with vomiting?
cards.a: Resuscitate and take to emergency surgery; avoid forceful taxis.

cards.q: Operation of choice for a child's inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Herniotomy alone (patent processus vaginalis, normal posterior wall).

cards.q: Standard open repair for an adult, and the older exam key?
cards.a: Lichtenstein mesh repair; older PYQs expected Bassini.

cards.q: Nerve most at risk in open versus laparoscopic repair?
cards.a: Open: ilioinguinal. Laparoscopic: lateral femoral cutaneous.

cards.q: Which triangle holds the external iliac vessels, and which the nerves?
cards.a: Doom holds the vessels; pain holds the nerves.

cards.q: Investigation of choice for an occult hernia?

cards.a: Sac excision; plus own-tissue wall repair; plus prosthetic mesh.
